findings.headline: Chief Finance Officer does not report directly to Chief Executive, contrary to CIPFA guidance
findings.detail: The Director of Finance and Revenues reports to the Deputy Chief Executive rather than the Chief Executive, which does not comply with CIPFA best practice for CFO independence. The council states that in practice the CFO can report directly to the CE when required and is involved in all financially significant decisions.
findings.matters: CIPFA guidance on CFO independence exists because a CFO reporting through another officer can create a barrier to escalating financial risks directly to the top of the organisation. While the council says this works in practice, it is a structural weakness that could slow communication of urgent financial issues.
findings.figures: No figures provided
findings.quote: The council does not strictly comply with this requirement in that the Director of Finance and Revenues reports to the Deputy Chief Executive; however, he is a member of the Management Team (which is the local comparison with the CIPFA Leadership Team reference)

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creates uncertainty and requires significant additional management capacity
findings.detail: The council is undergoing Local Government Reorganisation which needs to be completed on a tight timescale. The council has explicitly flagged the need to ensure sufficient capacity to manage the transition effectively while continuing to deliver services and maintain effective governance arrangements.
findings.matters: Major structural reorganisations create operational risk and distraction from core finance and service delivery. If capacity is insufficient, the council risks poor-quality transition planning, loss of institutional knowledge, and service disruption during a critical period.
findings.figures: Timeline not specified; described as 'very short timescale'
findings.quote: Local Government Reorganisation – LGR brings an array of opportunities and challenges that will need to be addressed in a very short timescale. It will be essential to ensure sufficient capacity is identified to look forward to challenge ways of working

findings.headline: Internal audit found control weaknesses in contract management and procurement compliance
findings.detail: A Corporate Governance internal audit review identified that while basic procurement training is in place, training needs to be expanded to cover bespoke procurement needs and broader contract management issues. Specific targeted training is now mandated for all contracting officers with a September 2026 deadline.
findings.matters: Weak procurement controls can lead to poor value for money on contracts, potential fraud, and inefficient service delivery. This directly affects the council's financial sustainability and spending efficiency.
findings.figures: Deadline for mandatory targeted procurement training: 30/09/2026
findings.quote: a Corporate Governance internal audit review identified that good progress has been made in providing training to officers who procure goods and services on behalf of the Council. However, it was recommended that this training be expanded to cover more bespoke procurement needs in services and wider contract management issues.

findings.headline: External auditor disclaimed opinion on 2024/25 accounts due to asset valuation control weaknesses
findings.detail: Ernst & Young issued a disclaimed opinion on the 2024/25 accounts because the council could not provide complete information to support property valuations in the balance sheet. The council says this has been addressed for 2025/26, but the fact that material asset values could not be verified represents a significant control weakness in financial reporting.
findings.matters: A disclaimed audit opinion means the auditor could not form a view on whether the accounts are true and fair. For a lender, this is a red flag on financial control and the reliability of the balance sheet, particularly for asset-backed borrowing decisions.
findings.figures: Property, Plant and Equipment assets – specific values not disclosed
findings.quote: EY issued a disclaimed opinion on that year's accounts... weaknesses in evidence to support some asset valuations were noted in their conclusion. This has been addressed for the 31st March 2026 valuations.

findings.headline: New Local Government Reorganisation Reserve being funded with unknown transition costs on top of £900k government grant
findings.detail: The council is setting up a dedicated LGR Reserve with planned contributions of £500k in each of 2026/27 and 2027/28. However, the paper explicitly states transition costs are currently unknown and may include programme management, IT separation, shadow authority costs, rebranding, legal setup, and backfilling. The £900k government grant per unitary covers only part of the cost; all other costs fall on the councils and new authority.
findings.matters: Local government reorganisation creates execution risk and absorbs management capacity at a critical moment; lenders to the new unitary will need to understand whether reorganisation costs constrain its opening financial position and what contingency exists
findings.figures: £500,000 per year 2026/27–2027/28 budgeted; £900,000 government grant; other costs unknown
findings.quote: A transfer into this reserve of £500,000 has been built into the MTFS for 2026/27 and 2027/28 to help with LGR transition costs. The level and exact nature of transition costs are currently an unknown but may include: Specialist programme management, Integration and separation of IT systems, Shadow authority election costs, Shadow authority running costs, Re-branding, communications etc., Legal & governance set up, Backfilling of costs. Each new unitary authority will receive £900,000 towards transition costs, but all other costs will be borne by the new unitary and the constituent councils.

findings.headline: Reactive maintenance costs jumped £197k whilst planned preventive maintenance fell £15k
findings.detail: Total property maintenance overran by £182k, but the breakdown reveals a shift from planned preventive work to reactive emergency repairs. The council is fighting fires rather than preventing them, a classic sign of infrastructure stress and deferred maintenance building up.
findings.matters: Deferring preventive maintenance typically accelerates future costs and signals the estate is no longer being managed proactively; lenders assess infrastructure condition as a proxy for management competence and future capital demand
findings.figures: £182,000 overspend: £197,000 reactive maintenance, £15,000 lower cyclical maintenance
findings.quote: The cost of maintenance of the Council's properties (excluding the Chantry Centre) for the year was £182,000 higher than budgeted. This is made up of additional reactive maintenance costs of £197,000 and lower planned (cyclical) maintenance of £15,000.

findings.headline: Benefits overpayment recovery fell £445k short of budget: declining caseloads and rising bad debt provisions
findings.detail: The council missed its income target for benefits overpayment recovery by £445k due to two factors: fewer cases to examine (declining caseloads mean fewer new overpayments identified) and higher bad debt provision (more existing overpayments now deemed uncollectable). Both signal the income stream is contracting.
findings.matters: Overpayment recovery is a controllable income stream; declining recovery combined with rising bad debt provisions indicates either administrative capacity issues or deteriorating collection prospects, both material to cash flow forecasting
findings.figures: £445,000 adverse variance
findings.quote: An increase to the level of the bad debt provision for the recovery of Benefits overpayments and a reduction in the identification and recovery of Benefits overpayments linked to reducing caseloads has resulted in an adverse variance of £445,000.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation costs overran by £331k, a demand-driven pressure the council cannot control
findings.detail: Spending on bed and breakfast and emergency accommodation exceeded budget by £331k after accounting for rent rebates. This is an uncontrollable, demand-driven cost that reflects homelessness pressures in the area. The paper does not flag this as temporary or one-off.
findings.matters: Homelessness-driven spending typically escalates and is unbudgetable; a lender needs to understand whether this is a structural trend in the council's locality and how it will affect the new unitary's finances
findings.quote: The net additional cost of bed & breakfast and emergency accommodation to the Council after taking into account rent rebates was £331,000.

findings.headline: Capital programme delivered 30% less than forecast in 2025/26, with largest slippage in Strategic Planning & Growth.
findings.detail: Actual capital spend was £12.5M against an estimate of £18.0M, a variance of £5.5M. Strategic Planning & Growth underperformed by £2.76M and Housing & Environmental Health by £882K. The council attributes variances mainly to timing of approvals and grant drawdown, but the scale suggests delivery challenges.
findings.matters: Persistent capital underspend indicates forecasting or delivery challenges; lenders need confidence that approved programmes are executed on plan.
findings.figures: £12.5M actual vs £18.0M estimate (variance £5.5M). Strategic Planning & Growth: £4.1M actual vs £6.9M estimate.
findings.quote: Overall, the Capital Programme has spent £12.5M against an estimate of £18.0M during the 2025/26 financial year.

findings.headline: £1.7M demolition project for Andover Former Magistrates Court approved in April 2026 with expenditure across 2026/27–2027/28.
findings.detail: Council approved a new capital commitment on 22 April 2026 for demolition and design work. This represents the largest single variance change in the updated programme and signals a material new capital outlay being brought into the 2026/27 and 2027/28 forecasts.
findings.matters: Major approved capital projects are key information for lenders assessing the council's capital programme delivery and financing headroom.
findings.figures: £1.7M budget; expenditure phased across 2026/27 and 2027/28.
findings.quote: The demolition of the Andover Former Magistrates Court and design work following demolition was approved by Council on 22nd April 2026. The budget of £1.7M is planned for expenditure across 2026/27 and 2027/28.

findings.headline: Levelling-Up Fund timing uncertainty is complicating capital receipts forecasting.
findings.detail: The council acknowledges that forecasting the Capital Receipts Reserve is 'more difficult than usual' due to unpredictability around Levelling-Up Fund grant timing and links to 'as yet unapproved' regeneration project costs. This creates material uncertainty in the financing strategy for future years.
findings.matters: Lenders need confidence in the council's ability to forecast capital resource availability; acknowledged uncertainty in major funding streams signals planning risk.
findings.figures: Capital Receipts Reserve forecast balance: £14.8M (April 2025) declining to £10.1M (March 2028).
findings.quote: Forecasting the future balance on the Capital Receipts Reserve is more difficult than usual due to the uncertainty of the timing of Levelling-Up Fund grant funding and its links to future, as yet unapproved, costs related to the delivery of regeneration projects.

findings.headline: Significant delays in asset maintenance project delivery during 2025/26
findings.detail: Multiple projects slipped from 2025/26 into 2026/27, including electrical infrastructure works in Andover High Street (delayed by parts availability), Multi Storey Car Park retention fees, church maintenance, and major Portway Depot refurbishment (£230k carried forward). While underspending can indicate budget over-estimation, the specific delays suggest execution risk and the potential for further slippage into 2027.
findings.matters: Repeated project delays raise questions about whether the £9.8M planned for 2026/27 will be fully deployed, and whether the reserve depletion trajectory is realistic or optimistic. If delivery slips again, the council may avoid spending the reserve but also defer asset maintenance, increasing long-term liabilities.
findings.figures: Portway Depot carry-forward: £230.9k; Electrical works (parts delay): £39.9k; Church/memorial works (survey delay): £27.9k; Green spaces: £15.6k; Sports facilities: £32.7k
findings.quote: Works for the electrical pop-up points in Andover High Street have been delayed due to the availability of parts. The works are scheduled to be completed by the end of June 2026.

findings.headline: Council acknowledges insufficient sustainable funding for Asset Management Plan
findings.detail: The risk assessment in the paper explicitly flags that ongoing AMP funding is not sustainable. Revenue contributions of £3.5M in 2026/27 cover only 35% of the planned £9.8M spending, with the gap covered by reserve drawdown. The paper states the need to 'seek sustainable funding' but identifies no solution.
findings.matters: This is the council's own assessment that current funding arrangements cannot continue. It indicates senior finance officers recognise the reserves will be depleted and that a funding model reset is needed—which typically means seeking increased revenue budget, capital receipts, or borrowing.
findings.figures: Revenue budget contribution 2026/27: £3.5M; Total AMP requirement 2026/27: £9.8M; Gap to be funded from reserve: £6.2M
findings.quote: There is a risk that there will be insufficient funds available to meet AMP requirements. The current level of the AMP reserve is sufficient to fund the programme included in this report; however, there continues to be the need to seek sustainable funding for the AMP.

findings.headline: Asset Management reserve forecast to fall 86% from £7.3M to £1.1M in a single year
findings.detail: The council's dedicated asset maintenance reserve is projected to drop from £7.344M at March 2026 to just £1.060M at March 2027. This depletion is driven by planned spending of £9.8M against revenue contributions of only £3.5M plus £31k in grants. Once this reserve is exhausted, the council will have no buffer for asset maintenance without either increasing revenue budget allocations or resorting to borrowing.
findings.matters: A council burning through asset reserves at this pace signals either severe accumulated maintenance backlogs being cleared, or systematic under-funding of asset maintenance. Either way, it indicates future budget pressure and potential credit risk if capital spending cannot be sustained.
findings.figures: Reserve balance 31 March 2026: £7.344M; Forecast 31 March 2027: £1.060M; Planned 2026/27 spending: £7.145M (land/buildings) + £2.035M (vehicles/plant) + £634.8k (IT) = £9.8M
findings.quote: At 31 March 2026 the Council's AMP reserve balances stood at £7.344M. It is expected that the reserve balance at 31st March 2027 will be £1.060M.

findings.paper_title: Annex 1 Annual Audit Report and Opinion
findings.headline: 75 of 182 historic audit actions from prior years remain unimplemented
findings.detail: Of 182 total audit actions agreed across 2023-24, 2024-25 and 2025-26, only 137 have been completed as of 31 March 2026. That leaves 45 actions pending, including control weaknesses related to revenue systems, business continuity, procurement processes, performance management, and backup resilience.
findings.matters: Audit actions represent agreed fixes to identified control weaknesses. A large backlog of unimplemented actions suggests either the council lacks capacity to fix problems, or has not prioritised them. This signals a slow-moving governance remediation cycle that a lender would want to monitor.
findings.figures: 137 of 182 actions completed (75%); 45 pending (25%). Current year 2025-26: 12 of 25 medium-risk actions pending after 31 March 2026 deadline.
findings.quote: 14 (17%) had been completed/closed, 43 (53%) were at varying stages of progress and 24 (29%) due for implementation after 31st March 2026.

findings.paper_title: Annex 1 Annual Audit Report and Opinion
findings.headline: Benefits overpayments are not being monitored or written off
findings.detail: The council identified that management is not actively tracking the total value of outstanding overpayments in council tax support and housing benefits, and that write-offs of overpayments are not being actioned. This means money owed to the council is sitting unrecovered and unaccounted for.
findings.matters: This directly affects the council's income recovery and cashflow. Outstanding overpayments represent money the council has spent but cannot recover. A lender would view unmanaged receivables as a sign of poor financial control and a drag on the council's financial position.
findings.figures: No specific amount quantified in the audit.
findings.quote: Management is not currently monitoring the level of outstanding overpayments. Write offs of overpayments are not being actioned.

findings.paper_title: Annex 1 Annual Audit Report and Opinion
findings.headline: Some Section 106 developer contributions not allocated within the legally binding agreement timelines
findings.detail: S106 contributions are money paid by developers to the council for infrastructure improvements, secured through planning agreements with specific time limits. The audit found that 'Some S106 funds received have not been committed within the defined period in the S106 agreement', meaning the council is holding developer money that should have been spent on specified projects. An Infrastructure Delivery Group has been established to address this, but the issue remains unresolved.
findings.matters: Failure to commit funds within agreement periods can lead to clawback (the developer gets the money back) or legal disputes. It also suggests the council is not effectively prioritising or executing infrastructure projects. For a lender, this indicates governance or execution weakness in capital project delivery.
findings.figures: No specific amount quantified; the audit notes the control weakness applies to 'older S106 contributions balances' and that options for management of older receipts are being developed.
findings.quote: Some S106 funds received have not been committed within the defined period in the S106 agreement.

findings.paper_title: Annex 1 Annual Audit Report and Opinion
findings.headline: Data backup and ransomware protection achieved only 'Reasonable Assurance', not 'Substantial', with testing gaps
findings.detail: The council's backup infrastructure has been tested only twice since deployment in February 2026. The audit identified that the council does not have an offline backup process (as advised by NCSC), making the backups potentially vulnerable to a ransomware attack that could compromise both the live systems and the backup copies.
findings.matters: Business continuity is essential for financial operations. If the council loses access to its finance, payroll, and benefits systems, it cannot function. A lender needs confidence that the council can recover from a major IT incident. This Reasonable Assurance rating (below the Substantial standard for most other areas) suggests higher-than-acceptable risk.
findings.figures: Only 2 test restores since February deployment; council has not implemented offline backup process despite NCSC guidance.
findings.quote: Only 2 test restores have taken place since the deployment of the backup infrastructure in February and the frequency of the backup restoration testing schedule may be inadequate for 2 councils. Protection of backups against ransomware attacks and technological failures is not optimised as advised by NCSC as it does not include an offline backup process.

findings.paper_title: Annex 1 Annual Audit Report and Opinion
findings.headline: The Lights theatre project has no completed financial forecast for ongoing revenue subsidy
findings.detail: The Lights (the council's new theatre/cultural venue) is transitioning to a new building with multiple governance and financial planning gaps. The audit explicitly notes that 'Further work is required to explore the revenue subsidy needed during the transition period' — meaning the council has not yet determined how much ongoing money it will need to put into the theatre after opening, or what the winding-down costs will be.
findings.matters: This is a significant capital commitment with incomplete financial planning. A lender would want to know the true cost of this asset before the council incurs it, and would be concerned about a major project being mobilised without a clear picture of future subsidy requirements.
findings.figures: No specific costs provided; the project has 'sufficient funding to cover the transition costs from Regeneration Programme reserves', but ongoing operational subsidy is unquantified.
findings.quote: Further work is required to explore the revenue subsidy needed during the transition period giving due regard to the risk appetite and the costs associated with winding down the current theatre.

findings.headline: Business rates reset impact managed through advance reserve planning
findings.detail: The council built a Collection Fund Equalisation Reserve in prior years in anticipation of a negative business rates reset. The reset occurred, with updated baseline levels released in the final Local Government Finance Settlement on 9 February. The impact has been built into the medium-term forecast.
findings.matters: Shows the council anticipated and planned for funding volatility; the risk has materialised but was manageable because reserves were built; £3M of this reserve is now being reallocated elsewhere
findings.figures: Final settlement released 9 February 2026; £3M of Collection Fund Equalisation Reserve being reallocated to asset management
findings.quote: In recent years, the Council has built a reserve in anticipation of needing to manage the impact of a negative outcome from a business rates re-set. That re-set has now happened, with updated baseline levels included in the final Local Government Finance Settlement that was released on 9th February.

findings.headline: Transformation costs for Local Government Reorganisation underestimated; reserve depletion accelerating
findings.detail: £1M was allocated to a new Transformation Reserve in February 2025, but is already recognised as insufficient for Local Government Reorganisation preparation costs. The budget now recommends adding £500,000 per annum across the medium term.
findings.matters: Structural reorganisation is approaching (2026/27) with escalating costs; shows early estimates were too low, and ongoing annual pressure will continue
findings.figures: £1M allocated Feb 2025; £500k p.a. additional now required
findings.quote: £1M was allocated to a new Transformation Reserve in February 2025. It is clear that this initial balance will be insufficient to meet the likely costs that will be incurred in preparation for LGR. This is recognised in this budget process with a further £500,000 per annum being included as an annual contribution to the reserve across the medium term.

findings.headline: Asset management programme underfunded; requires £1M additional annual contribution
findings.detail: The Asset Management Plan shows that current contribution levels to the reserve are insufficient to finance planned building repairs and fleet replacement sustainably. The budget recommends increasing the annual contribution by £1M per annum to address the shortfall.
findings.matters: Indicates historical underfunding of essential maintenance and asset replacement, now requiring correction; ongoing annual pressure
findings.figures: £1M p.a. additional contribution recommended
findings.quote: The Asset Management Plan report to Cabinet, included on this agenda, has shown that the current level of base contributions to the reserve will not be sufficient to sustainably finance the planned programme of building repair and fleet replacement. The recommendations in this budget report seek to address that shortfall by increasing the annual contribution by £1M per annum.

findings.headline: Regeneration programme has £3.18M funding shortfall being funded from reserves
findings.detail: A February 2024 report estimated the cost of delivering regeneration projects at over £70M. By February 2025, a shortfall of £3.18M had been identified to fully fund the programme. The budget now recommends increasing the Regeneration Reserve by this amount, meaning the capital programme relies on reserve draw-down.
findings.matters: Shows a major capital programme (£70M+) is not fully self-financing; gap relies on one-off reserves rather than recurring income
findings.figures: £70M+ estimated regeneration cost; £3.18M shortfall identified February 2025
findings.quote: In February 2025, there was an estimated shortfall of £3.18M to fully fund the programme. This budget report recommends increasing the balance on the Regeneration Reserve by this amount to fully fund that programme.

findings.headline: Council increasing annual AMP funding to £3.5M and transferring £3M from Collection Fund Equalisation Reserve
findings.detail: The council recommends increasing base-level annual AMP revenue funding to £3.5M for 2026/27 and future years, and simultaneously transferring £3M from the Collection Fund Equalisation Reserve to supplement AMP funding. Together these measures indicate previous funding levels were insufficient to support the required asset maintenance program.
findings.matters: Increases in committed revenue spending signal either rising asset deterioration costs or recognition of previous underfunding; combined with the need for inter-reserve transfers, this indicates the asset maintenance burden is exceeding what normal revenue sources can sustain
findings.figures: £3.5M annual revenue funding increase; £3M transfer from Collection Fund Equalisation Reserve
findings.quote: It is recommended that the base level of funding provided in the budget forecast is increased to £3.5M for 2026/27 and future years.

findings.headline: Asset Management Reserve forecast to decline from £3.7M to £0.8M by March 2027
findings.detail: The AMP reserve will decline from £3.716M at March 2025 to a forecast £799K by March 2027 after planned spending of £12.8M on maintenance and replacement. This minimal residual buffer leaves little capacity for unexpected repairs or deterioration beyond the approved plan.
findings.matters: Reserve adequacy is a key lending criterion; with annual AMP spending of £8.5M+, a residual of £0.8M provides almost no buffer for unexpected asset failures or infrastructure problems
findings.figures: Starting balance £3.716M, forecast ending £799K (all values in thousands)
findings.quote: Forecast Asset Management Reserve at 31st March 2027 799

findings.headline: Capital programme funding depends on asset sales where timing and value cannot be readily forecast
findings.detail: The council's long-term capital funding relies in part on receipts from asset disposals where both timing and extent are unpredictable. The report identifies this as a risk, with mitigation strategies including maximising external funding, cautious receipt valuations, and cash flow management to prevent scheme delays.
findings.matters: Dependence on unpredictable asset sales creates uncertainty about the timing and certainty of capital programme financing
findings.quote: The Council's ability to fund long term capital projects is, in part, reliant on receipts from disposal of assets where the timing and extent of the receipt cannot be readily forecast in advance.

findings.headline: Capital Receipts Reserve forecast to decline from £14.8m to £9.8m by March 2028
findings.detail: Combined Capital Receipts Reserve and related specific reserves totalled £14.841m as at 1 April 2025. After planned capital expenditure over the three-year programme, the balance is forecast to reach £9.865.7m by 31 March 2028. This represents a decline of approximately £5m over the programme period.
findings.matters: Declining capital reserves reduce the council's financial flexibility for new capital opportunities or responding to unexpected capital needs
findings.figures: £14.841m (opening balance 1 April 2025), £9.865.7m (forecast balance 31 March 2028)
findings.quote: The forecast balance on the Capital Receipts Reserve at 31 March 2028 is expected to be £9.9M. This is an increase of £1.4M from the level of the forecast in November 2025.

findings.headline: Chantry Centre improvement project approved with minimum cost estimate of £4m
findings.detail: Cabinet has approved £100,000 to appoint architects to develop design options to RIBA stage 2 for Chantry Centre improvements. Initial feasibility work indicates a minimum of £4m will be required for the full project. The council notes the design approval does not commit it to proceeding beyond RIBA stage 2.
findings.matters: A potential £4m capital commitment represents material future expenditure requiring financing and approval decisions by the council
findings.figures: £100,000 (design budget), £4M (estimated minimum cost)
findings.quote: The options put forward will cover a wide budget range, with estimates based on initial feasibility work indicating a minimum of £4M will be required.

findings.headline: Capital programme increased by £20m in three months, driven primarily by £11m in property development project changes
findings.detail: The three-year capital budget grew from £44,017.8k (November 2025) to £64,150.0k (February 2026). The largest movement was a net £11,066.9k increase in Property Development projects. Development costs for a proposed commercial property development were approved at Council on 3 December 2025 and are now reflected in the programme, with works anticipated to commence in 2026/27 and practical completion in 2027/28.
findings.matters: A £20m expansion of planned capital spending in three months reflects significant shifts in capital strategy and future financial commitments
findings.figures: £44,017.8k (November 2025 budget), £64,150.0k (February 2026 budget), £11,066.9k (net property development movement)
findings.quote: Net Movement in Property Development projects 11,066.9

findings.headline: Council already carries £7.45M in external debt from leisure centre and property investments
findings.detail: Test Valley has existing borrowing from two previous years: £5.9M borrowed in 2018/19 to part-fund the Andover Leisure Centre redevelopment, and £1.55M borrowed in April 2019 for a property purchase in Andover. The council is subject to Prudential Code limits on total borrowing.
findings.matters: Existing debt is a constraint on the council's ability to borrow further; PWLB lending is constrained by prudential limits based on existing commitments.
findings.figures: £5.9M (2018/19 leisure centre); £1.55M (April 2019 property purchase); total £7.45M
findings.quote: The Council borrowed £5.9M in 2018/19 to part fund the redevelopment of Andover Leisure Centre. In April 2019 a further £1.55M was borrowed to fund the purchase of property in Andover.

findings.headline: Internal borrowing of £6M planned for 2026/27-2027/28 with acknowledged timing risk
findings.detail: The capital funding plan includes £6M internal borrowing in each of 2026/27 and 2027/28. The strategy acknowledges risk in this approach: 'There is some risk with this approach as expenditure will be incurred before assets are sold and income is realised.' This means the council will spend money before it has generated the capital receipts to fund it.
findings.matters: Lenders care about timing mismatches between spending and income; if asset sales slip or valuations fall, the council could face a shortfall.
findings.figures: £6.000M internal borrowing for 2026/27 and 2027/28
findings.quote: Use of balances or internal borrowing will also be considered appropriate as a short-term measure where expenditure is made before expected capital receipts are generated. There is some risk with this approach as expenditure will be incurred before assets are sold and income is realised.

findings.headline: Capital expenditure peaks at £59.8M in 2027/28, heavily weighted to infrastructure regeneration
findings.detail: The capital programme shows a sharp spike in 2027/28 (£59.768M), with £39.126M allocated to infrastructure assets. This is driven by the Andover and Romsey regeneration programmes, which the document describes as 'ambitious' multi-phase projects. Much of this expenditure is still estimated rather than fully approved, making the forecast uncertain.
findings.matters: Lenders and finance officers need visibility on large capital commitments and their delivery risks; concentrated spending in a single year can create cash-flow and delivery challenges.
findings.figures: 2027/28 total £59.768M (up from £43.001M in 2026/27); infrastructure assets £39.126M
findings.quote: The next phases of the ambitious regeneration plans for both Andover and Romsey will be delivered throughout the period of this strategy.

findings.headline: Asset management reserve depleting rapidly: £3.7M to £799K in two years
findings.detail: The council's earmarked reserve for maintenance and asset replacement work will fall from £3.716M at 31 March 2025 to £799K by the end of March 2027. This sharp decline limits the council's ability to fund planned maintenance without revenue contributions or external funding.
findings.matters: Finance directors and lenders need to know whether the council can sustain asset maintenance spending; a depleted reserve signals potential future backlogs in maintenance of operational properties.
findings.quote: The balance on this reserve was £3.716M at 31st March 2025. Currently, it is forecast to have a balance of £799,000 remaining by the end of March 2027.

findings.headline: Capital receipts reserve forecast to fall from £9.9M to £1.1M by 2030/31
findings.detail: The council's useable capital receipts and funding reserves balance is projected to decline dramatically over the strategy period, from £9.865M at 31 March 2028 to just £1.072M by the end of 2030/31. This assumes no further external funding or capital receipts are identified. The council will become heavily dependent on achieving anticipated asset sales to fund future capital expenditure.
findings.matters: Lenders view shrinking reserves as a sign of deteriorating financial flexibility and increased vulnerability to unexpected costs or delays in asset disposals.
findings.figures: £9.865M to £1.072M by end of strategy period; opened with £14.8M at 1 April 2025
findings.quote: The forecast balance of the Capital Receipts and Funding Reserves used for the financing of the approved Capital Programme at 31 March 2028 is £9.865M. Unless further external funding or capital receipts are identified, this balance could reduce to £1.072M by the end of the period covered by this strategy.

findings.headline: Waste collection reform planned with no certainty on future costs or government funding
findings.detail: The council received £385,000 more than budgeted from the Extended Producer Responsibility scheme in the first six months, expecting this to continue. However, it explicitly states that further waste collection reform is coming with no visibility of either the costs the council will bear or what government support will be available.
findings.matters: Waste collection is both a significant budget item and a statutory duty. The council is flagging forward-looking uncertainty about an essential service—meaning it cannot yet size the budget impact of coming reform. This uncertainty will need to be resolved before a sustainable medium-term plan can be set.
findings.figures: £385,000 additional EPR income received in first six months; expected to continue in 2026/27; quantum and timing of future reform unknown
findings.quote: There is expected to be further reform to waste collection in future years, with no certainty as to the likely cost of provision or quantum of government support to deliver it

findings.headline: Housing Benefit overpayment recovery underperforming with growing bad debt provision
findings.detail: Benefits service shows an adverse variance of £332,000. Recovery of Housing Benefit overpayments is tracking lower than the council's own estimate at this point in the year, whilst simultaneously the council is having to increase its bad debt provision. Combined, these indicate both weaker cash collection than expected and a deteriorating view of collectability.
findings.matters: Lenders monitor cash flow quality. Shortfall in expected overpayment recovery and rising bad debt provisions together signal the council may be unable to realise income it has previously relied on, affecting available cash and requiring larger-than-expected write-offs.
findings.figures: £332,000 adverse variance in Benefits; lower than estimated recovery of Housing Benefit overpayments
findings.quote: identification and recovery of Housing Benefit overpayments being lower than estimated at this point in the year and a higher than budgeted provision for bad debts

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation costs continue to exceed budget due to rising demand
findings.detail: Housing & Environmental Health service reports an adverse variance of £152,000 to date. The council explicitly describes this as driven by increasing demand rather than service cost inflation, and characterises it as 'continuing', indicating this is not a one-off spike but an ongoing structural pressure.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is a statutory duty council's cannot avoid. A council's inability to absorb this demand within budget signals either deteriorating housing availability in the area or increasing vulnerability among the population it serves—both indicators of structural pressure that will recur.
findings.figures: £152,000 adverse variance; continuing higher than budgeted net temporary accommodation costs
findings.quote: continuing higher than budgeted net temporary accommodation costs driven by an increase in demand

findings.paper_title: Item 7 Annex 5 Medium Term Financial Strategy - Report
findings.headline: Business rates pooling arrangement withdrawn for 2026/27 after contributing £2M in 2025/26; risk-averse decision due to funding reset uncertainty
findings.detail: Test Valley is part of a business rates pool that has generated approximately £2M in net benefits in 2025/26. The council has decided not to continue in the pool for 2026/27 due to 'a combination of the uncertainty of a full re-set, with all accumulated growth expected to be removed; the risks of other parties' not achieving new growth; a new funding model for local authority funding more widely; and the introduction of a new rating list from April 2026.' No pooling income was assumed in 2026/27 forecasts, so there is 'no detriment to budget plans,' but the decision reflects the council's risk posture in an uncertain environment.
findings.matters: The loss of £2M in pooling gains from prior years, combined with the reset of all growth, shows how severely the business rates environment has deteriorated for this council.
findings.figures: 2025/26 pooling benefit: approximately £2M; 2026/27 pooling income: £0 (not in pool); no alternative income identified
findings.quote: It is estimated the pooling arrangements will be worth approximately £2M to the Council in the year...entering a business rates pool for 2026/27 will not be recommended unless there are unexpected incentives announced by the government

findings.paper_title: Item 7 Annex 5 Medium Term Financial Strategy - Report
findings.headline: Council Tax remains 29th lowest of 164 district councils in England; limited flexibility to raise income above maximum allowed increases
findings.detail: Test Valley's Council Tax is still very low: 29th lowest out of 164 district councils and 4th lowest in Hampshire. It is £45 (20%) lower than the average for England. The MTFS assumes annual increases of £5 per band D property. The council maintains a generous Council Tax Support scheme (100% relief for pensioners, up to 90% for working-age low-income households). Even at maximum allowable increases, Council Tax growth cannot close structural funding gaps.
findings.matters: Council Tax growth is constrained by referendum thresholds, and the council is already at a low baseline. This limits the ability to self-fund budget shortfalls through local taxation.
findings.figures: Current tax ranking: 29th lowest of 164 districts; £45 (20%) below national average; planned increase: £5 p.a. per band D
findings.quote: The current Council Tax charge is still very low when compared with other authorities – continuing to be the 29th lowest out of the 164 district councils in England, and the 4th lowest in Hampshire

findings.paper_title: Item 7 Annex 5 Medium Term Financial Strategy - Report
findings.headline: Budgets described as 'relatively stable' with 'only a small number of changes coming forward'; limited savings opportunities identified
findings.detail: A preliminary review with budget holders found 'the majority of budgets across the Council are relatively stable with only a small number of changes coming forward.' Temporary Accommodation costs are noted as rising rapidly and closely monitored, but the strategy contains no detailed savings plans for 2026/27 beyond items already scheduled (pension saving, EPR grant increase, one-off Council Tax surplus).
findings.matters: If budgets are largely locked in and demand pressures (particularly temporary accommodation) are rising, the council has limited options other than reserve draws or tax increases to balance budgets.
findings.figures: No specific savings figures identified; Temporary Accommodation cited as high-risk area requiring close monitoring
findings.quote: This has shown that the majority of budgets across the Council are relatively stable with only a small number of changes coming forward

findings.paper_title: Item 7 Annex 5 Medium Term Financial Strategy - Report
findings.headline: Reserve strategy now relying on Collection Fund Equalisation Reserve to manage budget gaps; council explicitly reserves right to increase draws
findings.detail: The strategy states that 'it is anticipated that the Collection Fund Equalisation Reserve will be used to manage any residual budget gap' for 2026/27. For the business rates reset, £1.53M is already planned to be drawn. The council notes 'the draw from this reserve could be increased to help close the budget gap if required.' This suggests reserves are being positioned as the primary shock absorber rather than identified savings.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion to cover structural budget shortfalls is a finite strategy. Once reserves are exhausted, there are no buffers for genuine shocks (pandemic, economic downturn, emergency costs).
findings.figures: Collection Fund Equalisation Reserve planned draw: initially £490k for funding gap, plus £1.53M for rates reset; potentially more
findings.quote: it is anticipated that the Collection Fund Equalisation Reserve will be used to manage any residual budget gap...The draw from this reserve could be increased to help close the budget gap if required

findings.paper_title: Item 7 Annex 5 Medium Term Financial Strategy - Report
findings.headline: Pension contribution rate falling from 17.7% to 14.7% delivers £670k p.a. saving, but this is a one-off benefit from triennial valuation
findings.detail: The Local Government Pension Scheme triennial valuation found asset levels exceed liabilities, allowing the employer contribution rate to drop 3 percentage points for the next three years. This saves approximately £670k per annum on a £28M pay bill. However, this is a temporary benefit: the next valuation will be in three years, and no similar saving is guaranteed to continue.
findings.matters: The council is treating this £670k saving as permanent in its medium-term forecasts, but it is explicitly temporary. Loss of this saving in 2029/30 would create an additional £670k budget pressure.
findings.figures: Rate reduction: 17.7% to 14.7% (3 percentage point saving); annual saving £670,000; pay bill context £28M
findings.quote: One of the outcomes of the triennial valuation is the setting of the employer contribution rate for the coming three years...a reduction of 3% from the current 17.7% rate and will result in a budget saving of approximately £670,000

findings.paper_title: Item 7 Annex 5 Medium Term Financial Strategy - Report
findings.headline: Council planning to bolster Transformation Reserve by £500k ahead of Local Government Reorganisation; uncertain total cost of transition
findings.detail: Test Valley is expected to cease to exist in 2028/29 following local government reorganisation. The council created a £1M Transformation Reserve in 2025/26 and now plans to add £500k to it for 'organisational development towards delivering transformational community-focused outcomes' and LGR preparation. The strategy notes it is 'likely that the reserve balance will need to be bolstered in the run-up to LGR but it does have sufficient balance to meet known obligations'—signalling uncertainty about total transition costs.
findings.matters: LGR creates a structural unknown: the council cannot predict its own end date or the scale of transformation costs. Reserve usage for transition costs is a competing priority against closing budget gaps.
findings.figures: Transformation Reserve balance: £1M opening; £500k growth planned for 2026/27; total anticipated need unclear
findings.quote: It is likely that the reserve balance will need to be bolstered in the run-up to LGR but it does have sufficient balance to meet known obligations

findings.paper_title: Item 7 Annex 5 Medium Term Financial Strategy - Report
findings.headline: Food waste implementation costs £850k annually but government funding level not yet confirmed; risk of underfunding in first year
findings.detail: The council introduced weekly food waste collections in October 2025 ahead of the April 2026 government mandate. Estimated annual cost is £850k. Government has committed to funding from April 2026 but has not indicated the level or duration. The risk is explicitly identified: 'there is a risk that this Council will not receive sufficient funding to cover the full costs.' The council notes it is 'likely' to rely on reserves for any shortfall.
findings.matters: A new service cost is being funded by the council before government funding is confirmed, creating a budget pressure that may fall on reserves if grant levels are insufficient.
findings.figures: Annual cost: £850,000; government funding level unknown; funds to come from April 2026
findings.quote: The estimated total cost of providing weekly food waste collections is £850,000 per annum. The amount of government funding is likely to be based on national formulae rather than calculated local need and there is a risk that this Council will not receive sufficient funding to cover the full costs

findings.paper_title: Item 7 Annex 5 Medium Term Financial Strategy - Report
findings.headline: Investment income falling £1.12M as interest rates decline; council assuming 3% long-term return vs. current rates
findings.detail: Actual investment income in 2024/25 was £4.92M; budgeted for 2025/26 at £4.40M; forecast to fall to £3.8M in 2026/27 as the Bank of England reduces rates toward the long-term 3% assumption. The council is 'using' the difference of £300k from its current forecast to close the budget gap, but this is a temporary offset to a permanent structural decline.
findings.matters: A significant income stream is permanently shrinking, removing a 'cushion' the council has relied on. Once rates reach 3%, this income will be locked at lower levels.
findings.figures: Investment income 2024/25 actual: £4.92M; 2025/26 budget: £4.40M; 2026/27 forecast: £3.8M (£1.12M decline from actual)
findings.quote: Actual investment income in 2024/25 was £4.92M and the budget for 2025/26 is £4.40M. Interest rates have started to fall...The figure forecast for 2026/27 was £3.5M

findings.paper_title: Item 7 Annex 5 Medium Term Financial Strategy - Report
findings.headline: Budget gap grows from £40k in 2026/27 to £3.91M cumulative over three years; 2027/28 alone shows £2.8M gap
findings.detail: Despite a nearly balanced budget for 2026/27 (£40k gap), the forecast balloons to £2.83M in 2027/28 and £1.08M in 2028/29. The document attributes this to 'easing of any mitigation from the funding review,' inflationary pressure on costs, and falling interest rate income. However, the council explicitly acknowledges 'very little reliance that can be placed on these forecasts until after the provisional settlement is released in December' due to funding uncertainty.
findings.matters: Growing budget gaps indicate the council faces an unsustainable cost base relative to forecast income, with no identified savings to close the gap beyond reserve usage.
findings.quote: Overall, the budget gap is forecast to grow from £40,000 in 2026/27 by £2.8M in 2027/28. A further increase of £1.1M is expected in 2028/29

findings.paper_title: Item 7 Annex 5 Medium Term Financial Strategy - Report
findings.headline: Business Rates Reset to strip £2.48M annual income; council planning £1.53M reserve draw to manage the shock
findings.detail: From 2026/27, all accumulated business rates growth since 2013/14 will be reset to new baseline levels. Test Valley's retained rates income drops from £5.73M in 2025/26 to £3.25M in 2026/27—a £2.48M loss. The council is forecasting a £1.529M draw from earmarked reserves plus £1M in assumed transitional support to manage this reset, and explicitly notes the draw 'could be increased to help close the budget gap if required.'
findings.matters: Business rates growth had been a reliable income stream for this council (it was 'one of the most successful in terms of growth'), and the reset eliminates that advantage entirely. Reserve depletion to cover permanent income loss signals limited medium-term flexibility.
findings.figures: Rates income drop: £5.73M to £3.25M (£2.48M loss); reserve draw £1.53M; transitional support £1M assumed
findings.quote: The impact of a full re-set was built into the medium-term forecast for 2026/27. The following table sets out the changes to retained rates income between years...Total Rates Income 11,566 [2025/26] 3,251 [2026/27]

findings.paper_title: Item 7 Annex 5 Medium Term Financial Strategy - Report
findings.headline: Core funding to fall 5–7% from April 2026 following government's Fair Funding Review; Test Valley specifically contacted as requiring 'bespoke treatment'
findings.detail: The Council's core spending power is forecast to reduce by £490,000 (to £14.245M) from a 7% cut to core funding, making this worse than the freeze facing most councils. MHCLG explicitly identified Test Valley as one of approximately 50 councils expecting the largest reductions, with the authority responding to oppose this approach in its consultation response.
findings.matters: A structural cut to core funding is a permanent change to the council's financial capacity, not a temporary pressure that can be absorbed through operational efficiency.
findings.figures: Core Spending Power forecast to reduce from £15.317M to £14.245M (7% reduction); Test Valley faces 5–7% cut versus funding freeze for others
findings.quote: Test Valley Borough Council will suffer a cut of between 5% and 7% in its core funding levels

news_drafts.headline: Chief Finance Officer does not report directly to Chief Executive, contrary to CIPFA guidance
news_drafts.lead: CIPFA guidance on CFO independence exists because a CFO reporting through another officer can create a barrier to escalating financial risks directly to the top of the organisation. While the council says this works in practice, it is a structural weakness…

news_drafts.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creates uncertainty and requires significant additional management capacity
news_drafts.lead: Major structural reorganisations create operational risk and distraction from core finance and service delivery. If capacity is insufficient, the council risks poor-quality transition planning, loss of institutional knowledge, and service disruption during…

news_drafts.headline: Internal audit found control weaknesses in contract management and procurement compliance
news_drafts.lead: Weak procurement controls can lead to poor value for money on contracts, potential fraud, and inefficient service delivery. This directly affects the council's financial sustainability and spending efficiency.
